svg.text: The acute abdomen: what not to do is half the nursing
Four ordinary kindnesses can kill a patient with a surgical abdomen.
Withhold until the surgeon has seen her
Food and fluid — she may need theatre,
and a full stomach makes anaesthesia unsafe.
Purgatives and enemas — they can rupture
an inflamed or obstructed bowel.
A hot water bottle on the abdomen —
heat hastens perforation.
All three feel helpful. All three do harm.
What the nurse should do
Nil by mouth, intravenous fluid, observations.
Record the pain: where it began, where it
is now, what makes it worse.
Give the prescribed analgesia. Withholding
it does not sharpen the diagnosis.
Keep her nil by mouth but not thirsty and
frightened — mouth care and explanation.
The pain that changes character
Appendicitis begins as vague pain around the navel and settles later into a sharp, localised pain in the right lower
abdomen. Sudden complete relief is not recovery — it usually means the appendix has burst and the pressure is gone.
Peritonitis follows within hours. Sudden relief in a surgical abdomen is an emergency, not good news.
A hernia that will not go back
A lump that becomes tender, tense and irreducible, with vomiting and no flatus passed, has trapped bowel inside it.
The blood supply is being strangled and the bowel dies within hours.
Never try to push it back. Nil by mouth, intravenous access, and call the surgeon now.
